FitDrive Buyer's Guide · Ford · 1961–2026

Ford Econoline / E-Series Buyer's Guide

America's van for 53 years — 8.2 million sold, best-seller from 1980 until the day the last one left the line, and still being built as a chassis the whole upfit industry runs on. From $1,881 flat-nose to Godzilla-powered box truck, sorted.

By Camille Bouchard · 4 chapters, about 8 min in all · Updated November 20, 2026 · Find one for sale

In this guide
  1. ●Overview
  2. 11961–1974
  3. 21975–1991
  4. 31992–2014
  5. 4Cutaway, 2015–

No vehicle in this library has a longer American service record. The Econoline arrived in 1961 as a flat-nosed Falcon with the engine between the seats, grew a truck frame in 1975, took the full-size-van sales crown in 1980 and kept it every single year until Ford retired the van in June 2014 — then refused to die, soldiering on as the cutaway chassis under the nation's box trucks, ambulances, shuttle buses and RVs. More than 8.2 million in total, making it the third-best-selling van line in history.

For buyers it is really 4 different machines: a genuine 1960s collectible, a 1970s–80s nostalgia wave that's just starting, the cheapest serious work van in America, and a brand-new chassis you can still order with a 7.3-liter V8. All of them share one virtue — there is nothing on them a local mechanic hasn't fixed a hundred times.

Quick picks

  • Best used work van: a 2009–2014 E-250 or E-350 with the 5.4 Triton — the final, most sorted years, built like anvils and priced like furniture.
  • The legend for fleets: a 7.3 Power Stroke diesel (1995–2003). Ambulance companies still fight over them; expect to pay for the privilege.
  • The collectible: a 1961–1967 flat-nose, pickup above all — the cab-over truck is the family's blue-chip piece.
  • The nostalgia play: a clean 1975–1991 Club Wagon Chateau, two-tone if possible. Nothing is more 1980s America, and prices are still kind.
  • The people-mover caution: 15-passenger wagons are cheap and useful — load them evenly, mind the tires, and skip roof cargo; their rollover record earned the warnings.

The chapters

Chapter 1The Box That Answered the Bus1961–1974 · First and second generations · From Falcon bones to V8 customs

Ford built America's answer to the VW Bus out of Falcon parts and sold it for $1,881. By 1974 the engine had moved forward, the V8 had moved in, and the custom-van decade had found its canvas.

2 min readChapter 2The Frame That Built an Industry1975–1991 · Third generation · Truck of the Year, then king of the hill

The first body-on-frame American van won Motor Trend's first-ever Truck of the Year, took the sales crown in 1980, and put a proper frame under every ambulance, shuttle and motorhome in the country.

2 min readChapter 323 Years of Default1992–2014 · Fourth generation vans · The best-seller that wouldn't quit

Motor Trend's 1992 Truck of the Year stayed in production for 23 years, best-selling full-size van in every one of them. It's now the cheapest serious work van in America — if you know which engine you're buying.

2 min readChapter 4The Van That Refused to Die2015–2026 · E-350 and E-450 cutaway · Still rolling at Avon Lake

The Transit took the van's job in 2014. The E-Series shrugged, kept its frame, picked up a 7.3-liter V8 named Godzilla, and still sells 30,000-plus chassis a year under box trucks, buses and motorhomes.
